entries.title: Carthage · Punic city and power
entries.location: Gulf of Tunis · present-day Tunisia, with wider Mediterranean connections
entries.note: A Phoenician-founded city developed into a major North African and Mediterranean power. The start is an approximate ninth-century plotting anchor, not the legendary foundation year treated as certain. Roman destruction in 146 BCE ended this selected Punic political phase; Roman Carthage later flourished on the site.

entries.title: Amazigh peoples · living cultures
entries.location: North Africa · communities across several present-day states and diasporas
entries.note: A selected modern reading window for diverse Indigenous North African communities and languages, not a date for their origins. Amazigh histories long predate the medieval dynasties and modern borders. Living heritage includes Zenete Ahellil traditions in Gourara; no single state or uniform identity is implied.

entries.title: Almoravid dynasty and realms
entries.location: Western Sahara, Morocco, parts of Algeria and Iberia
entries.note: A Sanhaja Amazigh movement established a realm linking Saharan routes, the Maghrib and al-Andalus. Uses UNESCO’s 1056–1147 dynastic convention. Other chronologies begin with the earlier movement or the later consolidation around Marrakesh; territorial control changed considerably.

entries.title: Almohad dynasty and realms
entries.location: Maghrib and al-Andalus · changing territories
entries.note: An Amazigh-led religious and political movement displaced Almoravid rule and expanded across the Maghrib. This window begins with the capture of Marrakesh, rather than the movement’s earlier beginnings. Its territorial losses and collapse unfolded in stages.

entries.title: Marinid Morocco
entries.location: Centred on Fez · present-day Morocco, with wider campaigns
entries.note: The Marinids developed Fez and sponsored architecture and learning. The plotting window follows the Met’s consolidated Moroccan ruling phase after the fall of Marrakesh; the dynasty’s earlier rise began before 1269. It did not govern the entire Maghrib continuously.

entries.title: Alaouite dynasty
entries.location: Morocco · changing political institutions and territorial authority
entries.note: A dynastic frame beginning with the conventional consolidation date. The continuation of the royal house is not uninterrupted independent government: French and Spanish protectorates overlapped it in the twentieth century. The modern constitutional state is a separate, overlapping reading.

entries.title: Morocco · French protectorate
entries.location: Much of present-day Morocco · distinct from the Spanish zones and Tangier
entries.note: The Treaty of Fez established the French protectorate. Spanish-controlled zones and Tangier had different arrangements; this block does not put all Morocco under one French jurisdiction. Moroccan institutions and resistance continued, and independence was recognised in 1956.

entries.title: Morocco · independent modern era
entries.location: Northwest Africa · Morocco
entries.note: 1956 marks the end of the French protectorate and recognition of independence, not the beginning of Moroccan society or monarchy. Decolonisation and territorial questions unfolded through several later stages; this date does not settle disputed boundaries.

entries.title: Hausa states · late medieval and early modern
entries.location: Hausaland · principally present-day northern Nigeria and southern Niger
entries.note: Kano, Katsina, Zaria, Gobir and other states developed distinct courts, markets and political histories. This selected phase starts with their documented ascendancy by the fifteenth century and ends at the start of the Sokoto jihad. It is not one Hausa empire, nor a claim that every state began in 1400 or disappeared in 1804.

entries.title: Sokoto Caliphate
entries.location: Central Sahel · principally present-day northern Nigeria and neighbouring regions
entries.note: A jihad beginning in 1804 transformed the regional political order and established a multiethnic network of emirates. Enslavement and slave labour were central to its economy. British conquest ended independent caliphal authority in 1903; communities and some emirate institutions continued under changed conditions.

entries.title: Hausa communities · continuing histories
entries.location: Northern Nigeria, southern Niger, wider West Africa and diasporas
entries.note: A selected modern window, not an origin date. Hausa-speaking communities continued through colonial rule and independence across state boundaries. Kano’s living Durbar traditions exemplify cultural transmission and adaptation; neither the Sokoto Caliphate nor colonial Nigeria contains the whole Hausa story.

entries.title: Zulu Kingdom · independent phase
entries.location: Southeastern Africa · present-day KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa
entries.note: Shaka and subsequent rulers consolidated a kingdom through alliances and force. The dates delimit the selected independent political phase to British military defeat and partition. Later resistance and institutional changes continued; 1879 did not end Zulu people or culture.

entries.title: Zulu communities · colonial and modern histories
entries.location: South Africa · especially KwaZulu-Natal, with wider communities
entries.note: This reading begins at the loss of the kingdom’s independence to make continuing history visible, not to date the origins of Zulu identity. Communities, isiZulu and royal institutions persisted through colonialism, apartheid and democratic South Africa. Language, cultural identity and political allegiance are not interchangeable.

entries.title: Madagascar · early settlement networks
entries.location: Madagascar, the Comoros and western Indian Ocean connections
entries.note: Archaeology, crops, languages and ancestry reveal African and Southeast Asian contributions to Malagasy histories. Late-first- and early-second-millennium settlements provide an important evidence window. The first human arrival, earlier foraging evidence and the timing of different migrations remain debated; 600 is not a proven first landing, and 1200 is not an end to settlement.

entries.title: Maroserana, Sakalava and Mahafaly kingdoms
entries.location: Western and southern Madagascar
entries.note: Maroserana-associated rulers consolidated several kingdoms, including Menabé and Boina, among diverse local communities. This selected seventeenth- and eighteenth-century window shows political formation and expansion, not a single island-wide state. The end of the window does not end Sakalava or Mahafaly communities and institutions.

entries.title: Merina kingdoms and Kingdom of Madagascar
entries.dates: c. 1600–1897 CE · changing kingdoms and monarchy
entries.location: Central highlands and, later, much of Madagascar
entries.note: A broad frame for highland consolidation, subsequent division and late-eighteenth-century reunification, followed by wider expansion. Not all Madagascar was always under Merina control. France annexed the island in 1896; 1897 marks the monarchy’s final colonial removal, not the disappearance of Merina communities.

entries.title: Madagascar · French colonial rule and transition
entries.location: Madagascar · changing colonial and autonomous arrangements
entries.note: French annexation in 1896 opened this selected colonial frame. Resistance, coercion and institutional change belong within it. The republic proclaimed in 1958 preceded full independence in 1960, so these dates do not describe one unchanging legal arrangement.

entries.title: Madagascar · independent eras
entries.location: Madagascar · Indian Ocean
entries.note: Independence was proclaimed on 26 June 1960. This frame includes successive republican and political eras rather than one uninterrupted regime. Malagasy cultural histories extend across and before these modern constitutional boundaries.

entries.title: Igbo-Ukwu · archaeological metalwork
entries.location: Southeastern Nigeria · Igbo-Ukwu
entries.note: Excavated ritual and burial contexts contain sophisticated copper-alloy vessels, regalia and imported beads. The range is an approximate archaeological plotting window; the ninth-century dating has been debated. It does not identify a documented empire or date the beginning or end of Igbo history.

entries.title: Swahili peoples and coastal cultures
entries.dates: c. 9th century CE–present · broad cultural frame
entries.location: East African coast, islands and wider Indian Ocean connections
entries.note: A broad reading frame for African coastal communities participating in Indian Ocean exchange, not a single empire. Kilwa is one selected city, not the whole coast. Coastal cultures and Kiswahili-speaking communities continued through Portuguese, Omani and European colonial interventions and remain living traditions, as at Lamu.

entries.title: Yoruba communities · living cultures
entries.location: Nigeria, Benin, Togo and wider diasporas
entries.note: A selected modern reading window, not an origin date. Yoruba histories extend beyond the political phases of Ife and Oyo. Osun-Osogbo’s living sacred landscape and evolving annual festival are one example of continuing cultural practice; no single faith or state represents all Yoruba people.

entries.title: Edo communities · continuing Benin traditions
entries.location: Benin City and wider Edo communities · Nigeria and diasporas
entries.note: The selected frame begins with British conquest and looting to show that Edo society and artistic traditions continued afterwards. The cultural community and royal institution are not the same as the formerly independent state. This is unrelated to the modern Republic of Benin’s name.

entries.title: Shona communities · living cultures
entries.location: Zimbabwe and neighbouring countries, with wider diasporas
entries.note: A selected modern window, not a date for the origins of Shona communities. Great Zimbabwe’s medieval urban phase is one part of a longer regional history. Living mbira traditions illustrate continuity and change, and are also practised by communities other than Shona; no uniform state or unchanging identity is implied.
